title: States-in-Waiting
abstract: After the Second World War, national self-determination became a recognized international norm, yet it only extended to former colonies. Groups within postcolonial states that made alternative sovereign claims were disregarded or actively suppressed. Showcasing their contested histories, Lydia Walker offers a powerful counternarrative of global decolonization, highlighting little-known regions, marginalized individuals, and their hidden (or lost) archives. She depicts the personal connections that linked disparate nationalist struggles across the globe through advocacy networks, demonstrating that these advocates had their own agendas and allegiances, which, she argues, could undermine the autonomy of the claimants they supported. By foregrounding particular nationalist movements in South Asia and Southern Africa and their transnational advocacy networks, States-in-Waiting illuminates the un-endings of decolonization—the unfinished and improvised ways that the state-centric international system replaced empire, which left certain claims of sovereignty perpetually awaiting recognition. This title is also available as Open Access on Cambridge Core.

Conceptually, the work connects to History and Geography. The book was recognised: ACLS Open Access Book Prize & Arcadia Open Access Publishing Award finalist (2026) — History.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

States-in-Waiting has already achieved unusually strong scholarly traction for a 2024 book, with 24 OpenAlex citations placing it in the top 1% of works in its field and year. Its open-access availability, 963 downloads, and recorded teaching-related video discussions indicate both active academic use and broader circulation.

Full narrative

Lydia Walker’s States-in-Waiting offers a counternarrative to familiar accounts of decolonization by tracing how alternative sovereign claims within postcolonial states were often overlooked, suppressed, or rendered illegible in the international order after the Second World War. Published by Cambridge University Press in the Global and International History series, the book is grounded in history and geography and has clearly resonated with scholars working across imperial, postcolonial, and political histories.

The clearest sign of impact is scholarly uptake: the book has 24 citations in OpenAlex, a level that places it in the top 1% of works in its field and year. The citing literature is diverse but coherent, appearing in journals and books concerned with decolonization, sovereignty, borderlands, and postcolonial politics. Recent citing works show the book being used to frame studies of Naga sovereignty, Vietnamese identity, decolonization as dissent, and legal recognition of communities, suggesting that it is helping to organize conversations well beyond a single regional case.

The book is also reaching readers through open access and teaching-oriented channels. OpenAIRE records both a closed publisher version and an open instance, and the book has 963 downloads and 485 views in the available usage record. In addition, it has been discussed in three recorded YouTube talks hosted by academic or scholarly institutions, which points to its role as a pedagogical anchor and as a text that is being introduced to wider audiences through public-facing scholarly programming.

Other signals reinforce that profile. Library holdings and WorldCat presence show institutional acquisition, while a LibraryThing record notes it as a finalist for the ACLS Open Access Book Prize and Arcadia Open Access Publishing Award in History. The book is also associated with the Sustainable Development Goal of Reduced inequalities, aligning with its concern for marginalized political claims and unequal recognition in international history. Overall, the record shows a book with strong academic uptake, clear teaching relevance, and growing visibility through open-access distribution.
